newsitem.title: RWANDA: Canadian priest slain in Rwanda during Sunday mass.
newsitem.headline: Canadian priest slain in Rwanda during Sunday mass.

text.p: An unidentified gunman shot and killed a Canadian Roman Catholic priest during Sunday mass in northwestern Rwanda, a Canadian diplomat and Rwandan officials said.

Father Guy Pinard, 61, was gunned down as he was handing out communion at his parish church in Kampanga village, 20 km (12 miles) north of the northwestern regional capital of Ruhengeri, the officials said.

They speculated the killing was carried out by Hutus who returned late last year from Zaire or Tanzania and feared he would recognise and denounce them as killers during the three -month genocide of an estimated 800,000 people in 1994.
Claude Dusaidi, an advisor to Vice President and Defence Minister Major-General Paul Kagame, said Picard, a missionary had lived in Rwanda for more than 30 years and remained during the genocide.

Canadian Consul Gerald Ohlsen confirmed the killing and told Reuters there were probably more than 200 Canadians resident in Rwanda and all non-essential workers had previously been advised to leave the country.
"We will now consider issuing another type of warning," he said.
Pinard's death was first announced by Pope John Paul, who told pilgrims in St Peter's Square he had been "barbarically assassinated this morning while celebrating mass at his parish church."
"Let us pray to the Holy Virgin for him, for those who are dear to him and for his people, that they may again find peace and respect for life", he added.
Pinard was from Trois Riveres in Canada's Quebec province and was a member of the White Fathers missionary order.
A spokesman for the White Fathers in Rome said Pinard had been in Rwanda since 1962. The order was seeking further details about the circumstances of the killing.
"He was killed during communion but we don't know how...We don't know if he was killed by a madman," the spokesman said.

Suspected Hutu militiamen killed three Spanish aid workers in cold blood in the town of Ruhengeri two weeks ago and wounded an American in one of his legs in an attack on the compound where they lived. Gunmen stormed a house where the aid
workers were staying and demanded their passports before shooting the three Spaniards -- two men and a woman nurse -- at close range in their heads.
Rwandan officials said troops killed some 80 people in a crackdown in Ruhengeri prefecture following the killings.
After the attack, the United Nations said aid work in Ruhengeri would be limited to the daytime and expatriate workers would not be allowed to spend a night in the city, close to Zaire's border.

A U.N. report said on Friday Hutu death squads were killing Tutsi survivors of genocide and witnesses, who were forced to move out of remote areas to places near army positions and towns in search of security.

The report by the U.N. human rights office said survivors were being hunted down in their homes, intimidated, threatened and sometimes poisoned in remote areas of in the tiny central African country bordering Zaire.
The U.N. report said at least 227 genocide survivors were killed in 1996, when attacks against them rose sharply, and urged Rwanda to take measures to protect them.
Hutu militia among 600,000 refugees who returned from Zaire late in 1996 were behind some of the attacks, the report said.
The mass influx from eastern Zaire and the expulsion of half a million Hutu refugees in Tanzania by troops in December have increased ethnic tensions in Rwanda with the Tutsi minority.
